title: Average Net Worth at 30–33 in the U.S. (2026): where do you rank?
excerpt: The median net worth for people aged 30–33 in the U.S. is $68,000; the top 10% starts at $440,000. Type yours and see your percentile — no account needed. Full p10–p90 ladder by age and city.
content_html:
Net worth for people aged 30–33 in the U.S.

Total assets minus total debts — bank accounts, investments, retirement accounts and home equity, less mortgages, loans and cards.

Modeled estimate · federal survey data

Household-level figures: the underlying survey (Fed SCF) measures households, grouped by the reference person's age — combined for a couple, and they read high for a single person. Why, and how this changes as live data grows.

Half of people aged 30–33 in the U.S. have a net worth above $68,000. Reaching the upper quarter takes about $235,000, and the top 10% starts at $440,000 — roughly 6.5× the median. The lower quarter sits below $7,100, and the bottom 10% is negative — more owed than owned.

Common questions

What is the median net worth for people aged 30–33 in the U.S.?

The median net worth for people aged 30–33 in the U.S. is $68,000. Half of this group is above that figure and half below.

What net worth puts you in the top 10% of people aged 30–33 in the U.S.?

About $440,000. The 90th percentile is the level only one in ten people in this group exceeds — roughly 6.5× the median.

Where do these numbers come from?

They are modeled percentile distributions fitted to this cohort from federal survey microdata — the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances (released October 2026), the BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey, Census ACS and BLS wage data — and they blend toward anonymized, aggregated data from Keeping Up members as each cohort grows. Full methodology at keepingup.com/methodology.

How this is built. Percentiles are modeled for this cohort from federal survey microdata — the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances (released October 2026), the BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey (2024), the Census American Community Survey and BLS Occupational Employment & Wage Statistics (May 2025) — with metro cost-of-living and wage adjustments. As Keeping Up members in this cohort grow, the band blends toward anonymized, aggregated live data (minimum cohort sizes apply; no individual is ever identifiable). Seeded figures are household-level, as in the SCF; live cohorts are individual-level. Amounts are in current dollars. Read the full methodology.

Last updated October 2026. Cohort: people aged 30–33 in the U.S.. Model sample basis: 500.
